title: ‘The Worst I’ve Ever Seen’: Cargo Thefts Have Turned Violent in Pursuit of AI Hardware
gist: Cargo thieves have begun deliberately immobilizing private security escort vehicles — via hit-and-run rear-endings and PIT maneuvers — on Silicon Valley to Southern California shipments of AI data center hardware, with millions of dollars in gear never recovered. Verisk CargoNet data shows reported theft counts fell 26 percent year over year last quarter while the value taken more than doubled, and the dominant attack vector is not force but fraud: hijacked or illegally resold federal motor carrier numbers that let criminals book loads as a legitimate long-standing trucking company.

themes.theme: Escorts as targets: the violent escalation

insights.claim: Two recent shipments of high-value technology traveling from Silicon Valley to Southern California lost their private security escorts to deliberate vehicular attacks — one escort was rear-ended in a hit-and-run, the other was spun out by a PIT maneuver — after which both semitrucks continued to unknown destinations and were never heard from again.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Physical interdiction of armed-escort logistics is a step change in risk for AI hardware in transit, and it will reprice both escort services and cargo insurance for the segment.
insights.locator: The incidents involved two different shipments of high-value technology

insights.claim: A former Los Angeles sheriff's detective with 25 years investigating truck cargo theft describes current conditions as the worst he has seen nationwide, citing simultaneous escalation in methods, value extracted, and frequency.
insights.speaker: Gerardo Pachuca
insights.so_what: A practitioner with a quarter-century baseline calling a regime change is a stronger signal than any single incident statistic.
insights.quote: The methods they are using, the value they are getting, the frequency these crimes are occurring.

insights.claim: Industry investigators assume the truck drivers in the escort attacks were complicit in the scheme, describing insider participation as an increasingly common issue in freight crime.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Insider collusion defeats perimeter and escort security entirely, which shifts the effective control point to driver vetting and identity verification.
insights.locator: Pachuca, Coughlin, and Ramon all say that no one was hurt

insights.claim: The escort industry has shifted from a seasonal to a year-round business, with liquid cooling parts, servers, and computer chips now the largest client category for at least one operator that has protected 13,000 shipments over four years without a loss.
insights.speaker: Michael Duffy
insights.so_what: Physical security is becoming a recurring line item in AI infrastructure capex — a small but fast-growing services market attached to the data center buildout.
insights.quote: Now that the values have shot through the roof, we’re getting called all the time,
insights.locator: Michael Duffy, CEO of Solutions Group International

themes.theme: The AI buildout as a new theft surface

insights.claim: Total spending on AI data center construction in just the first half of this year surpassed the total for all of 2025, creating the concentration of high-value, thinly protected freight that thieves have redirected toward.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: The capex curve is steep enough that its second-order effects — theft, insurance, security services — are now material enough to appear as operating friction in the buildout.
insights.locator: More recently, the booming AI data center industry has created a new target

insights.claim: Cargo crime is consolidating rather than growing: Verisk CargoNet data released this month shows reported theft counts last quarter fell 26 percent year over year while the value of goods taken more than doubled, as criminals concentrate on expensive cargo.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Headline incident counts now understate the loss exposure by a wide margin — the right metric for insurers and shippers is value-at-risk per load, not frequency.
insights.locator: While the overall number of thefts reported last quarter fell 26 percent

insights.claim: The structural vulnerability is that copper, metals, and enterprise-grade computer and networking equipment move under standard freight procedures, creating what Verisk CargoNet calls a significant mismatch between their financial value and their ordinary transportation and security profile.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: The value/security-profile mismatch is the single best screen for which cargo classes get hit next as component prices rise.
insights.quote: a significant mismatch between their financial value and their ordinary transportation and security profile,
insights.locator: These shipments are typically transported according to standard procedures

insights.claim: Documented AI-adjacent losses span the full component stack: 34,560 optical transceiver cables and 96 network switch modules taken in April en route from Olive Branch, Mississippi to Richardson, Texas; a $4 million May seizure including Deepcool AI data center cooling equipment; $2.2 million recovered in June including eight pallets of Celestica-manufactured server switches for Meta worth $550,000; and a $1 million trailer of data center equipment found near Chicago.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Optics, switches, and cooling — not GPUs — are what is actually moving in bulk and getting stolen, which maps the real physical supply chain of the buildout.
insights.locator: In April, for example, thieves allegedly made off with 34,560 optical transceiver cables

themes.theme: Identity fraud, not force, is the real attack vector

insights.claim: Most cargo heists require no physical breach at all — criminals exploit the fragmented freight market in which hundreds of thousands of independent owner-operators sign up online for shipments, then hack a truck operator's email via social engineering or phishing to take over the business and book loads under its legitimate motor vehicle registrations.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Freight theft has become a cybersecurity problem, which means the effective countermeasure is carrier identity verification, not locks, guards, or escorts.
insights.locator: For the most part, today’s cargo heists are relatively simple

insights.claim: The specific enabling mechanism is illegal resale of motor carrier numbers — the federal identifiers assigned to trucking companies — which hands fraudsters a long-standing permit, phone number, and email address; both recent escort-targeting thefts and the Meta switch theft involved recently sold motor carrier numbers.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Recently transferred motor carrier numbers are a concrete, screenable red flag that shippers and brokers can act on today — the highest-leverage control available.
insights.locator: In another version of the scam, freight industry experts say

insights.claim: GPS trackers on stolen trucks can be spoofed or deactivated, leaving no trace, which is why telematics-based load monitoring fails against organized crews.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Tracking-based security offers false assurance against sophisticated actors; only tamper-evident or covert trackers attached to the goods themselves retain value.
insights.locator: Criminals sometimes hack into a truck operator's email address

insights.claim: The federal response is MOTUS, a new system designed to let trucking companies manage their registrations and customers verify legitimacy, backed by a March regulatory bulletin reminding the industry that registration numbers may only be sold as part of corporate transactions and that such sales must be reported.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Registration verification infrastructure is the regulatory chokepoint; MOTUS adoption rates are the metric that determines whether this theft wave persists.
insights.locator: A new federal system, called MOTUS

insights.claim: The National Motor Freight Traffic Association's cybersecurity director characterizes the perpetrators as very sophisticated, very organized criminal organizations rather than opportunistic thieves.
insights.speaker: Ben Wilkens
insights.so_what: Organized-crime framing raises the ceiling on both loss severity and the eventual law-enforcement response, including federal task-force involvement.
insights.quote: These are very sophisticated, very organized criminal organizations,
insights.locator: These are very sophisticated, very organized criminal organizations

themes.theme: Attempt rates, underreporting, and insurance distortion

insights.claim: A Georgia-based shipper detects a scammer attempting to steal one of its loads every single day, and despite employee training and a paid monitoring service loses cargo roughly once a month when employees get sloppy — most recently $650,000 worth of tools.
insights.speaker: Jaclyn Giles
insights.so_what: A daily attempt rate against a single mid-size shipper is the base rate that matters — this is continuous adversarial pressure, not episodic crime.
insights.locator: Georgia-based shipper FLS Transportation Services detects a scammer

insights.claim: Official theft statistics are structurally understated because some carriers decline to report thefts for fear their insurance costs will skyrocket, while others respond by buying supplemental insurance or splitting loads across many trailers to cap per-incident losses.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Reported loss data is censored by insurance incentives, so both the true frequency and the insurance repricing ahead of it are larger than published figures imply.
insights.locator: Some carriers don’t report thefts partly because of fears

insights.claim: Countermeasures are spreading down to physical surveillance and identity checks: shippers now attach GPS trackers directly to high-value loads including LEGO toys, one freight client deployed Flock license-plate cameras and discovered would-be thieves casing its yard to identify the highest-value trailers, another began scanning to catch fake drivers' licenses, and Tesla enhanced driver identity checks after trailers with millions of dollars in batteries were taken from its loading docks.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Surveillance and identity-verification vendors have a fast-forming market in logistics yards — Flock-style license-plate networks and ID scanning are the products being pulled in.
insights.locator: Giles says FLS now attaches GPS trackers directly to high-value shipments

insights.claim: Recovery frequently depends on luck rather than detection — California Highway Patrol's $2.2 million recovery began with a tip from a prospective buyer who thought a deal was too good to be true.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: With interdiction depending on buyer conscience, the effective recovery rate is low enough that prevention economics dominate — assume the goods are gone.
insights.locator: In June, California Highway Patrol received a tip

themes.theme: Export controls create the fencing market

insights.claim: US export controls on chips and other high-value technology create the incentive to steal and smuggle the goods to countries like China, and location pings observed when some stolen parts are activated lead freight industry experts to suspect many shipments are taken overseas.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Export restrictions raise the grey-market premium enough to fund organized theft — an unpriced enforcement cost of the chip control regime and a channel worth monitoring for diversion.
insights.locator: US export controls on chips and other high-value tech

insights.claim: A decades-long history of freight deregulation combined with state-by-state reporting standards and low prosecution rates makes cargo theft a very high-reward, low-risk crime — described flatly by a trade body official as easy money.
insights.speaker: Ben Wilkens
insights.so_what: Until prosecution rates or reporting standards change, the risk-adjusted return to the criminal side keeps rising with hardware prices — expect the trend to persist through the buildout.
insights.quote: Reporting structures and standards vary from one state to another, and the prosecution rates are low enough that this is a very high-reward, low-risk crime,
insights.locator: Preventing these crimes has been complicated by a decades-long history
